questions.topic: The gold ground of the San Vitale apse, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: explain why a gold mosaic ground refuses recession and what that does to the figures on it

stimulus.body: A short reference note on the gold ground of the san vitale apse, ravenna is set for a close-reading task. It states: A gold ground is not a description of any lit surface; it is a decision about what kind of space the image inhabits. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a surface with no shadow and no drawn architecture can tell you about how far back a figure stands. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: Keeping “explain why a gold mosaic ground refuses recession and what that does to the figures on it / Ask what a surface with no shadow…” in view, which answer is supported rather than assumed?

options.text: It creates a deep illusionistic space, since the even courses of tesserae make the gold behave like a receding floor and wall
options.misconception: believes a regular gold mosaic ground produces illusionistic recession, when gold is exactly what denies it

options.text: It holds the figures in a shallow, non-receding field, so the scene reads as a presentation rather than a place with depth
It cancels the modelling of the figures, since a featureless ground removes the light and shade the faces depend upon
options.misconception: supposes a plain ground destroys modelling, when the modelling is carried by the tesserae of the bodies themselves

options.text: It locates the procession inside a real building, since gold glass in mosaic was only ever used to record a sunlit interior
options.misconception: treats gold as a way of rendering a lit room rather than a way of suspending place

questions.explanation: A gold ground is not a description of any lit surface; it is a decision about what kind of space the image inhabits. Because the field is even in value, carries no cast shadow, and is interrupted by no drawn architecture, it supplies no cue for distance, and the figures therefore have nothing to recede from. They stand forward on a surface that reads as the limit of the image rather than as the floor of a room. The effect on the subject is direct. Justinian is not shown standing in a church; he is shown holding a bowl of bread, and the gold takes that offering out of any particular hour and place and gives it the character of a presentation, a thing offered to be looked at and not merely recorded. Note the negative half of the reasoning too. The modelling of the faces and drapery is not weak but very strong, worked in graded rows of tesserae that shift in value, so a plain ground does not flatten a mosaic; it isolates the bodies that stand on it. And because the field denies depth, it also denies architecture, which is why the setting of this apse is supplied by the actual curve of the half-dome and by the light entering its clerestory windows rather than by anything painted.
questions.hint: Ask what a surface with no shadow and no drawn architecture can tell you about how far back a figure stands.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The hem of the Theodora panel at San Vitale
questions.learningObjective: describe how the lower edge of a Byzantine mosaic carries a second subject

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: The hem of Theodora's robe is a second picture, and it is the clearest case in early Byzantine mosaic of a field that is a boundary also being used as a place. A marginal reminder adds: ask whether the small shapes at the hem are a repeating ornament or can be resolved into figures with clothes and feet. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: The passage invites “describe how the lower edge of a Byzantine mosaic carries a second subject / Ask whether the small shapes at the hem are a…”. Which option is the evidence-backed one?

options.text: Fixing the scale of the empress, since tiny figures at the hem give a standard for measuring how large she is
options.misconception: treats "Fixing the scale of the empress, since tiny…" as if it followed from the evidence

options.text: Carrying a second subject, since the three figures at the hem read as a procession that extends the imagery down into the border
Recording the cost of the robe, since a list of small devices would show the value of the material and its embroidery
options.misconception: reads a figural border as an inventory of value, as though it itemised price rather than told a story

options.text: Signing the work, since a craftsman places a miniature self-portrait in the border of a commission he finished
options.misconception: treats a border figure as a maker's signature, a convention the mosaic does not use

questions.explanation: The hem of Theodora's robe is a second picture, and it is the clearest case in early Byzantine mosaic of a field that is a boundary also being used as a place. A pattern of white gem shapes alone would be ornament, and ornament at an edge has the job of stopping the eye from sliding out of the composition. But three of those shapes resolve into coloured cloaks and feet, and they read as a procession moving along the lower edge. Once that happens the border becomes a place with its own subject, and the image gains a second register without a second frame. The device does several things at once. It turns the hem of a garment into a landscape, so the empress's robe becomes the ground on which something happens, and the second subject is drawn at the scale appropriate to its position, small because it is far away and low, not small because it is unimportant. It also connects the two facing panels: the Justinian panel opposite has soldiers and a very thin, dark architectural strip at its base, so the lower zone of the whole apse carries architecture on one side and a figural procession on the other. And it refuses the idea that a border is inert ground. The two are the same thing here, and the eye is given a second thing to read precisely where a tapestry or a painted panel would have given it a stop.
questions.hint: Ask whether the small shapes at the hem are a repeating ornament or can be resolved into figures with clothes and feet.

questions.topic: The youthful shepherd in the Galla Placidia mosaics, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: explain why the Good Shepherd in a fifth-century mosaic is beardless and monumental

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the youthful shepherd in the galla placidia mosaics, ravenna. the gold tunic and the frontality are doing the work, and the missing beard is part of the same decision. A marginal reminder adds: ask whether the figure reads as someone tending sheep or as someone who rules, and what the missing beard contributes. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The rule to carry into this item is “explain why the Good Shepherd in a fifth-century mosaic is beardless and monumental / Ask whether the figure reads as someone…”. Which option applies it?

options.text: It shows that the mosaic was copied from a Roman sarcophagus, since imperial dress and frontal pose are what Roman reliefs do
options.misconception: jumps from a shared convention to a copied source, where a convention needs no borrowing

options.text: It presents the shepherd as a ruler rather than a herdsman, so the image claims that power and salvation are shown in the same figure
It argues for a classical subject, since a beardless shepherd is the Greek type and the gold is the Roman type
options.misconception: treats beard and gold as proof of two sources rather than as one deliberate blend

options.text: It identifies the patron, since a beardless young ruler in gold must be the dead princess shown as a shepherd
options.misconception: reads a conventional divine type as a specific portrait of the patron

questions.explanation: The gold tunic and the frontality are doing the work, and the missing beard is part of the same decision. In a fifth-century mosaic a shepherd rendered as a beardless youth in gold is not a farmer; it is a statement about authority, and the size of the figure in a field of other figures sets that authority at the same level as everything else on the ceiling rather than above it. The four rivers below complete the argument without any further explanation, because in this imagery flowing water is the sign of the paradise the shepherd rules, and the rock from which they issue is the same rock that stands for the whole commanded place. Three things this image is not doing are worth separating out. It is not a portrait of the princess whose name the mausoleum takes, because a divine type is being shown rather than a person, and the details of the type are conventional. It is not evidence that a Roman sarcophagus was copied, because imperial dress and frontality were current Byzantine practice and a convention travels without a source. And it is not a lesson on two subjects, Greek and Roman, in one figure, because the youth and the gold are read together as a single statement. The test to apply is simple: if a viewer could not name the patron from this figure, but every viewer would read authority from it, the figure is a type and its scale is part of its meaning.
questions.hint: Ask whether the figure reads as someone tending sheep or as someone who rules, and what the missing beard contributes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Encaustic handling in the Sinai icon of the Virgin and Child
questions.learningObjective: distinguish encaustic panel painting from the gold-ground convention

stimulus.body: A short reference note on encaustic handling in the sinai icon of the virgin and child is set for a close-reading task. It states: Two things are being read at once, and they are different kinds of evidence. A marginal reminder adds: ask what wax bound paint can do that a gilded ground cannot, and what a plain background is doing to the space. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: With “distinguish encaustic panel painting from the gold-ground convention / Ask what wax bound paint can do that a gilded ground…” settled, which choice remains consistent with the text?

options.text: That the icon is a copy, since original panel icons of that century are always painted on a gold ground
options.misconception: treats a single convention as a test of originality rather than one option among several

options.text: That the icon was made for private devotion rather than for a church, since a plain ground removes the altar function
options.misconception: supposes function follows from the ground colour, when a work can be made for a church in any convention

options.text: That the painter worked in wax on wood with a brush, and that the modelled flesh records a painter trained where modelled portraiture was practised
That the icon is unfinished, since a background of plain brown is what remains when a gold layer has been lost
options.misconception: reads a deliberate plain ground as lost gilding rather than as a choice

questions.explanation: Two things are being read at once, and they are different kinds of evidence. The first is medium and technique. Encaustic is pigment bound in hot wax and applied with a brush, and the marks it leaves can be modelled: laid in, blended while warm, and then picked out in opaque light. That is what the description reports in the cheeks, the brows and the chain of highlights down the nose. A gold ground, by contrast, is a different kind of decision about surface, and its absence here is not a loss. A background of plain warm brown pushes the figures forward and lets the modelling do the work, so the two are alternatives rather than stages of one method. The second thing is training. Faces modelled with light and shade, and faces with the fronts lit from one side and shadows in the other, belong to a pictorial world in which such modelling was practised; the saints here wear late antique dress, and the Virgin is enthroned frontally with the Child at her breast, which is a subject not derived from the same tradition as the shading. The church the icon came from is Byzantine and gold-grounded in its other panels, which is exactly why the difference is informative. An image that models flesh against plain ground in a gold-grounded church is making a deliberate choice about how the person is to be seen, not recording a local shortage.
questions.hint: Ask what wax bound paint can do that a gilded ground cannot, and what a plain background is doing to the space.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Continuous narrative in the Vienna Genesis
questions.learningObjective: explain how a continuous narrative scroll handles several moments in one field

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: The device is called continuous narrative, and its logic is that a single continuous zone of landscape or architecture holds several moments at once. A marginal reminder adds: ask why the painter repeats a figure instead of drawing two separate frames, and what the repeated figure is for. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: Set against “explain how a continuous narrative scroll handles several moments in one field / Ask why the painter repeats a figure instead of…”, which choice is actually backed by the text?

options.text: To identify a single moment precisely, since the painter worked to make each episode self-contained for a reader in a hurry
options.misconception: supposes repetition serves isolation, when it is what makes a sequence legible

options.text: To read a sequence left to right, since the repetition of figures separates a set of episodes that share one continuous landscape
To compare two different artists, since a change of costume and of handling between episodes marks a change of hand
options.misconception: reads variation inside one zone as evidence of several hands without any comparison

options.text: To infer that the manuscript is unfinished, since a painted zone should never contain a figure more than once
options.misconception: treats a compositional rule of some books as a test of completion everywhere

questions.explanation: The device is called continuous narrative, and its logic is that a single continuous zone of landscape or architecture holds several moments at once. Because the same personage recurs, the eye has to be taught how to separate them, and it is taught by the things that do not recur: a wall, a door, a strip of ground, a shift in the pattern of a garment. A reader trained on this book learns to scan a band of landscape and to register each appearance of a figure as a new moment, so the order is given by the layout rather than by separate frames. Two consequences follow, and they are the reason the device matters. First, the book becomes a sequence in a very literal sense, so the reader experiences a story unfolding across a surface rather than turning from compartment to compartment, and the physical experience of a codex page is a landscape read sideways. Second, repetition is not a failure of economy but the mechanism, which is why the criterion for a competent rendering in this technique is not individual figure quality but whether each episode is separable. The purple ground is a separate matter and should not be confused with any of this. It is the costliest support available, dyed before the vellum was written on, and it is a statement about the value of the book and the rank of its patron rather than about how the episodes are laid out. Nor does a figure appearing twice in a zone tell you a hand changed, because a change of hand is argued by comparison with other pages, not by a costume that is deliberately the same.
questions.hint: Ask why the painter repeats a figure instead of drawing two separate frames, and what the repeated figure is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Silver ink and decorative initials in the Rossano Gospels
questions.learningObjective: explain why a manuscript's ornament can carry as much weight as its pictures

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about silver ink and decorative initials in the rossano gospels. this book is a useful corrective to the habit of expecting pictures. A marginal reminder adds: ask where the ornament sits relative to the text, and what a book with no pictures is still doing. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The standard for this item is “explain why a manuscript's ornament can carry as much weight as its pictures / Ask where the ornament sits relative to the text,…”. Which option meets the standard?

options.text: That the book is unfinished, since a Gospel book of that century ought to have carried evangelist portraits and does not
options.misconception: reads one book's omissions as damage, when several books of the period have no portraits

options.text: That the animal forms are symbolic of the evangelists, since a man and a lion always denote Matthew and Mark
options.misconception: applies an evangelist-symbol code to decorative initials that are not portraits of anything

options.text: That the text is unimportant, since a book that spends its effort on decoration must be valued for its ornament alone
options.misconception: substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for the relation the passage establishes

options.text: That writing itself is the image, so effort has been spent on the letterforms and their frames rather than on figures beside the text

questions.explanation: This book is a useful corrective to the habit of expecting pictures. Some of the earliest Gospel manuscripts are essentially illuminations of the script itself: the text is carried by letters of a monumental size, and the ornamental energy goes into the opening letters, which are laid out as tiled fields of interlaced animals, birds, vine scrolls and small heads, each compartment given its own ground colour and separated from its neighbours by a wide bar. What that does is shift the image from something beside the text to the text's own shape, so that reading is a visual act as well as a verbal one. The right response to the absence of portraits is therefore neither to call the book defective nor to suppose the text was secondary. This is a luxury object: purple and gold grounds, silver ink and dense ornament together are what a patron of rank can be shown, and the way to demonstrate that here is to make the letters themselves magnificent. The animal forms are the trap in this question, because a trained viewer reaches for the evangelist code, in which a winged man, a lion, an ox and an eagle stand for Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Inside a tiled initial those forms are part of a patterning with no narrative function, and a lion in a compartment of a letter is not Mark. The test to apply: ask what the decoration is attached to. Attached to the text, it is the argument for this book; placed in a separate picture, it would be an illustration; and a manuscript that has no pictures at all is not therefore a manuscript without an image.
questions.hint: Ask where the ornament sits relative to the text, and what a book with no pictures is still doing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The registers of a Sanchi stupa gateway
questions.learningObjective: read a carved gateway as an ordered statement of a Buddhist cosmos

stimulus.body: A short reference note on the registers of a sanchi stupa gateway is set for a close-reading task. It states: A gateway at a stupa is not primarily a door. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a course of small figures is for on a monument whose real content is a dome and a railing. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: This question asks the reader to use “read a carved gateway as an ordered statement of a Buddhist cosmos / Ask what a course of small figures is for on a monument…”. Which option results?

options.text: Presenting the gateway as an ordered cosmos, with the animals and the emblems of the teaching at the top and narrative below
Showing that the gateway was rebuilt, since three courses can only be the record of three separate building campaigns
options.misconception: counts courses and infers campaigns, which nothing in a course count supports

options.text: Imitating a wooden gate, since stacking horizontal beams is a way of copying carpentry in stone
options.misconception: settles on a derivation from timber without evidence that the courses borrow anything

options.text: Making the structure lighter, since each course is set back from the one below and the load appears to decrease upwards
options.misconception: reads a symbolic programme as a structural device, when the courses are not working that way

questions.explanation: A gateway at a stupa is not primarily a door. It is a carved statement about what the monument encloses, and the statement is organised vertically. The elephants at the outer ends and the emblems above the central pillar, a wheel for the teaching itself and a three-pronged sign associated with the community that keeps it, sit at the top and the centre; below them run the narrative courses, and the lowest register carries the smallest and most numerous figures. Read that way, the gateway is doing three separate jobs at once. It gives the stupa an architectural face, so that the dome and the railing are announced at ground level to a visitor standing in front. It supplies a scale, because the courses are filled with figures of a known sort, from worshippers to gods, and a human figure is the only ruler in a set of symbols that would otherwise have no size at all. And it makes the enclosure legible as a sacred place before anyone enters it. The distractors each name a real property of a stacked course and then read it wrongly. Courses set back from one another do not lighten a stone gateway; the structure is a straight post carrying a straight beam, and the projection is a matter of cross-section, not of load. A count of three does not record three campaigns. And while stone does imitate timber elsewhere in the world, nothing about three courses establishes that, and a derivation claim needs evidence beyond the fact of resemblance. The gateway works because it is a diagram with figures in it, not because of anything it copies.
questions.hint: Ask what a course of small figures is for on a monument whose real content is a dome and a railing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The four hands of the Chola bronze of Shiva as Lord of Dance
questions.learningObjective: account for how a bronze encodes a sequence of acts in one standing figure

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: Four arms is not a compositional problem in a tradition that has assigned an object and a gesture to each of them. A marginal reminder adds: ask whether each hand and foot is specified, and what a reader gets from the combination. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: Working from “account for how a bronze encodes a sequence of acts in one standing figure / Ask whether each hand and foot is specified, and…”, which answer is consistent with the note?

options.text: The scale of the figure, since a small dwarf at the foot sets the size of the god and makes extra arms read as motion
options.misconception: attributes the readability of a multi-armed figure to relative scale, which does nothing for it

options.text: A small number of copies, since a four-armed figure is only workable where a workshop held the same pattern unchanged
options.misconception: supposes a codified ensemble depends on workshop uniformity rather than on convention

options.text: The loss of the lower arms, since bronze cast in more than one pour often loses a projecting limb and leaves the pose tidier
options.misconception: explains a deliberate, balanced design as a casting loss that never occurred

options.text: A set of fixed attributes, since the ring of flame, the gestures and the objects are a codified system and the ensemble is read as a whole

questions.explanation: Four arms is not a compositional problem in a tradition that has assigned an object and a gesture to each of them. What the ensemble records is a sequence: the drum that makes the first sound, the flame that will consume, the outward palm that allays fear, the pointed foot that offers refuge, and the dwarf of illusion pinned under the advancing foot. Each element is specified, and the specification is what makes the image legible. Because every element is fixed, the figure can be read at three levels at once, and viewers do read it at three levels. There is a narrative, in which creation and destruction happen and the god's foot tramples what misleads. There is a doctrinal reading, in which the same figure holds together the roles the tradition assigns to Shiva. And there is a bodily reading, in which the lifting of the left foot and the flying hair make the body a moving thing rather than a static column, which is why the bronze is not a support for the composition but the composition. Two of the wrong answers here are worth picking apart, because each names a real feature. A codified ensemble does not require a workshop that never varied the pattern, since copies in different metals and different sizes are exactly what a set of fixed attributes produces. And a dwarf at the foot is not there to measure anything; the ring of flame already supplies a measure, and the dwarf is there to be overcome. The bronze was also cast, not lost in a pour, and nothing about it suggests a missing limb.
questions.hint: Ask whether each hand and foot is specified, and what a reader gets from the combination.

questions.topic: The absence of a figure on the Book of Kells Chi Rho page
questions.learningObjective: explain an all-ornamental page as a decision about how a text is to be entered

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the absence of a figure on the book of kells chi rho page. the right way to read this page is as a decision about how a reader begins. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a reader has to do on this page that an ordinary page of text does not ask of them. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: In an attribution dossier on the absence of a figure on the book of kells chi rho page, which statement about it agrees with the note?

options.text: It makes entering the text an act of looking, since the letters themselves are the image and the reader must resolve the pattern to read
It marks the loss of an original, since a page at the opening of a Gospel would certainly have carried a picture of the author
options.misconception: selects "It marks the loss of an original, since a page at…" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

options.text: It reserves the letters for the scribe and the ornament for another hand, since two different hands are visible in the page
options.misconception: converts a distribution of labour into an omission of a figure

options.text: It anticipates a change of subject, since a page with no figure prepares the reader for the narrative that follows
options.misconception: reads a decorative opening as foreshadowing a narrative, which it does not contain

questions.explanation: The right way to read this page is as a decision about how a reader begins. The first words of the Gospel are set out as a single field of interlace, and the field is organized so that a reader who knows the words sees them immediately and a reader who does not has to hunt for them inside a thicket of knots and spirals. The cat and mouse forms, the repeated border creatures and the abstracted human and animal heads embedded in the letters are not decoration around the text; they are what the text is made of. This is the opposite of the usual economy of an image, where a picture interprets a text quickly, and it changes the position of the reader from someone receiving a summary to someone doing work. The temptation in every direction is to supply a missing thing. It is tempting to say a picture of Matthew has been lost here, but the book is not short of pictures and this page is surrounded by them. It is tempting to see two hands, one for the letters and one for the pattern, but a book of this kind is a collaborative object throughout and nothing in the page marks a division. And it is tempting to read the page as preparation for a story, when the point of it is not narrative at all. The test to apply is functional: ask what the reader has to do here that they would not have to do on an ordinary text page. The answer is that they must look carefully, which is exactly the behaviour an opening page can ask for.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has to do on this page that an ordinary page of text does not ask of them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The inhabited initial of the Lindisfarne Gospels incipit
questions.learningObjective: read a letter as a building containing figures

stimulus.body: A short reference note on the inhabited initial of the lindisfarne gospels incipit is set for a close-reading task. It states: The initial is doing the work of a frontispiece inside a letter. A marginal reminder adds: ask which single attribute on the page belongs to one evangelist and to no other. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The prompt gives “read a letter as a building containing figures / Ask which single attribute on the page belongs to one evangelist and to no…” as the nudge. Which option is really supported?

options.text: The colour of the ground behind the initial, since different evangelists are introduced on grounds of different hues
options.misconception: invents a colour code between evangelists that the page does not use

options.text: The winged man inside the letter, since the evangelist's own symbol settles who the following text is by, and it sits inside the structure of the text
The number of animals in the grid, since a fixed number belongs to each of the four evangelists
options.misconception: posits an arithmetic of animals per evangelist with nothing behind it

options.text: The knot pattern, since the tightness of the interlace records how early the book is and so dates the text it introduces
options.misconception: treats decorative complexity as a chronological index, which it is not

questions.explanation: The initial is doing the work of a frontispiece inside a letter. A winged man is the attribute attached to Matthew alone among the four evangelists, and a reader meeting it knows before reading a line who the following book is by. What makes the placement remarkable is that the figure is not placed beside the text but inside the structure of the text, occupying the bowl of the letter, so the identification is delivered in the form the reader is about to use. That is what inhabited initials do generally: they convert the opening of a book into a set of small pictures attached to the letters rather than to the page. The surrounding grid, with its interlace, its knotwork and its animals, is not a code and not a clock. There is no established link between a particular knot density and a particular date, so an argument that tightens from a knot pattern is arguing about a style and should be labelled as one. There is no colour code assigning a hue to each evangelist, and there is no fixed number of animals per evangelist. Both of those are the kind of detail a reader invents when a page is elaborate enough to seem systematic. The one thing to note about the beasts elsewhere on the page is that they are shown in conflict, in combat, or in the grip of an order, which is a statement about a world the manuscript imagines rather than an ornament to be decoded.
questions.hint: Ask which single attribute on the page belongs to one evangelist and to no other.

questions.topic: The uncoloured drawing of the Utrecht Psalter
questions.learningObjective: explain what a monochrome pen drawing is for in a working book

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: These are the characteristics of a pattern book, and each of them points the same way. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a second book that repeats the first book's drawings almost exactly is evidence of. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: For a gallery handout about the uncoloured drawing of the utrecht psalter, which answer is supported rather than assumed?

options.text: A work of severe economy, since the absence of colour records a shortage of pigments in the scriptorium that produced them
options.misconception: reads a working method as a shortage, when the later copy is equally uncoloured

options.text: An early stage of a book that was never finished, since the pages were left ready for a colourist who never came
options.misconception: substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for the relation the passage establishes

options.text: A printed design, since a drawing that can be repeated exactly must have been traced from a printed model
options.misconception: confuses repeatability with print, when a pattern was traced from a pattern before it

options.text: Reproducible working copies, since a book of sketches could be traced and carried from workshop to workshop without any need to finish the pages

questions.explanation: These are the characteristics of a pattern book, and each of them points the same way. The drawing is in line rather than in colour, which means the whole design can be put down with one tool. The handling is quick and repetitive, so an entire psalm can be shown in a small number of consistent strokes. The book was made beside others in the same workshop in the same manner, which is what happens when a group of monks is being trained to draw. And the decisive evidence is the near copy: a second volume about thirty years later repeats the drawings so closely that the second was plainly traced from the first, or from a common exemplar. The inscription is a documentary act, and a dated signature tells you what the commissioning party recorded, which in a monastic context is normally the date of the contract or of the dedication rather than the hour the last gold leaf was burnished. It is a strong piece of evidence and it has a proper use: it fixes the object in time. The style is a different kind of evidence and it answers a different question. The three failures in the distractors are each a common overreach. A signature is not a guarantee about the minute of execution, and it can in principle be copied, which is a reason to test it rather than a reason to discard it. A shared convention is not a shared workshop. And the claim that both kinds of evidence are useless commits the opposite error to credulity: an inscription and a stylistic comparison each carry real weight, they simply carry it on separate questions, and an attribution built from both is stronger than one built from either.

A free leg that touches lightly is a controlled outcome, not an ambiguous casting, and the figure is finished and finished with care. And the pose works with no landscape at all, which is exactly what a free-standing figure for a courtyard needs: a bronze that depended on a horizon could not be carried around or set anywhere. Here the ground is broken, and because it is broken the figures belong to different orders rather than to one place. The horse and the dragon are the encounter, and they are drawn to fill the shape they are in. The princess and her retinue occupy a band that is flatter and quieter, as though the spectacle is being watched from a place outside it. Nor does one habit identify a painter, since the same omission can be a habit of a workshop, a taste, or a solution to a narrow field. It states: Three elements in this scroll do three different jobs, and keeping them apart is the whole analysis. A marginal reminder adds: ask which element gives the rock its size and which element breaks the mass in two. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

options.misconception: treats a staffage detail as a record of travel rather than as a measuring device

The rock mass is nearly the entire field, and its surface is not smooth: it is built from a dense grain of short strokes that reads as the resistance of stone rather than as light falling on it. The mist is a band of emptiness cut across the middle, and its function is interruption. It breaks a single mass into two, so that the summit above it can be read as separate in space from the base below it, and it is the reason the eye can move up the sheet instead of stopping at the foot. The travellers are the smallest thing in the picture, and they are not there to be looked at. They are a measure, and a very efficient one: because they are the only part of the image at a known size, the rock can be read as enormous without any other device. Nothing is competing, because the figures are too small to hold the eye against the mass. The three wrong readings each turn a formal device into a claim it cannot support. A party of travellers is not a route; painters of this kind used such parties constantly, in mountains with no roads. A band of mist establishes that the two masses are separated, not how far apart they are. And a handscroll or hanging scroll is not a set of panels to be rearranged, because the sequence of its content is the sequence in which it is read, and reordering it destroys it.

A written statement on the sheet, made by or for someone close to the making, is a claim about a moment in time. A stylistic feature is a claim about a body of work, and it will date a sheet to a range, not to a year. So where both are present, the colophon is doing the finer work, and the style is being used to check it: does this sheet's handling, the way the near rock is textured, the way the leafless trees are built from downturned strokes, the way the far bank is dissolved into a few lines, agree with what is known of that date and place? A high viewpoint looking down into a valley, a middle grove, and a far bank reduced by mist is a way of building a landscape in layers so that the eye can travel through it, and the same three-part scheme recurs in works of many dates. The three wrong answers are all cases of promoting a feature to a date. Colour was used in both of the schools that divide this output, so it discriminates between practices and not between centuries. Winter trees were a permitted subject, not a signature of a period. And an older manner is not automatically an earlier one, quite apart from the fact that a dissolve into mist is a technique rather than a period. The test: ask whether the evidence names a year or names a family of work.

options.text: Narrating, since each register carries a separate episode in the life of the Virgin and the order of the rows is the order of the story
options.misconception: mistakes a surface feature of "Narrating, since each register carries a…" for the governing rule

options.text: Measuring, since a small figure at the foot of a large one is a scale bar from which the heights can be calculated

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: The two halves are about a constraint and about a consequence, and the mechanism has to be stated precisely. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a painter cannot undo once the plaster has dried, and what that does to his freedom to revise. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

options.text: It forces the eye to commit before the whole is visible, and the corrections become part of the surface, so the wall records a sequence of decisions and not a single resolved design
It guarantees a consistent result, since a painter who must finish each day cannot change his mind and so the plan is preserved intact
options.misconception: supposes a deadline removes the possibility of a change of mind

options.text: It has no effect at all, since a wall can be re-plastered and repainted at any time and so imposes no real constraint on the painter
options.misconception: treats a finished wall as a reversible surface it is not

questions.explanation: The two halves are about a constraint and about a consequence, and the mechanism has to be stated precisely. Paint applied to wet plaster becomes part of the wall as it dries, so a working day is a unit of irreversible commitment: whatever is laid on in the morning is part of the wall by the evening. That has two practical effects and one theoretical one. Practically, the painter has to know the whole design at the start, because he cannot erase a figure he has finished in order to fit it into a composition he has not yet reached; the drawing for the wall is therefore settled in advance and transferred across it, which is why a wall of this kind carries a full preparatory scheme and why the joins between the day-areas can often be found as slight tonal changes. Practically again, and this is the harder case, a figure that has to join a wall already painted has to be adjusted on the spot, and a record of corrections is not a sign of incompetence but of a decision made under a deadline. Theoretically, the day-areas are also a record of who was in the workshop and when, because the sequence of areas follows the sequence of the design and the seasons of the year limit how much of the wall can be done before the plaster is no longer workable. So the finished wall is a palimpsest of decisions in an order, and a survey that can find that order can find the chronology of the work. Two errors to reject. A deadline does not prevent a change of mind, it prices one, and a correction is the cheapest possible form of it. And a wall cannot be re-plastered at will; that is a different technique requiring the removal of what is there. The last is a category error: a day is a unit of commitment, not a unit of elapsed time.
questions.hint: Ask what a painter cannot undo once the plaster has dried, and what that does to his freedom to revise.

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by the registers themselves, and it is a narrative order and a spatial one at the same time. The upper band carries the story of the parents of the Virgin, which is the necessary beginning: their marriage, the announcement, the long childlessness, the journey to the town, and the events that make the birth possible. Without that the cycle has no starting point, and the painters put it at the top so that a reader's eye enters the story at its highest point and descends. The middle band then carries the infancy and life of Christ, from the birth through the childhood to the ministry, which is the part that needs the parents behind it. And the lower band carries the Passion, which is the part a chapel like this exists to show, put at eye level and below so that it is met on the way in and on the way out, and running the length of both side walls. The separate scene at the entrance wall, where the dead and the living are separated, closes the whole sequence and is placed where a visitor leaving the chapel passes it last. So the cycle is read in one direction, from the highest register down and around to the entrance, and the arrangement is itself an argument: the story of salvation descends, literally, onto the person standing in the room.

questions.topic: Why a gold apse denies the space the emperor occupies
questions.learningObjective: explain how a decorative surface makes a claim about presence

stimulus.body: A short reference note on why a gold apse denies the space the emperor occupies is set for a close-reading task. It states: An explanation of this kind has to work in two halves, because the question has two. A marginal reminder adds: ask what a surface with no cues for distance can do for a scene that needs to happen somewhere. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: One operative hint guides this question: “explain how a decorative surface makes a claim about presence / Ask what a surface with no cues for distance can do for a scene…”. Which choice obeys it?

answer.exemplar: Begin with what the mosaic actually offers the eye. There is a gold field laid in even courses behind and beneath the figures, no cast shadow anywhere on it, and no drawn building, and the apse is a curved half-dome with a band of windows above it. That is all. The gold is a surface and it is even: it supplies no cue for distance, no horizon and no floor, so the figures have nothing to recede from. The refusal is not a failure of technique; a mosaic of this period could render a receding pavement or a shadowed interior perfectly well, and the artists who made the apse were among the most capable in Europe. It is a decision about what kind of space the image occupies. Three things follow from it, and they are the substance of the answer. First, the space becomes a presentation rather than a place. Justinian is not standing in a church on a particular afternoon; he is holding a bowl of bread and offering it, and the gold takes the offering out of any hour and place, which is exactly what a figure in an apse above an altar needs to do, because an apse is a place of offering and the image states the offering rather than depicting it. Second, the gold flattens the distinction between the real and the represented. The real light of the apse falls on the mosaic from the windows above, and the mosaic answers it with a field that has no light of its own, so the light in the room and the light in the picture are two systems that meet at the surface. That is a theological claim about a boundary, made in material. Third, it removes the possibility of hierarchy by scale. In a space with a floor, a taller figure would be a nearer one, and a smaller one a further one, and rank would have to be argued by other means. On a gold field, size is free, and the emperor can be as large as he needs to be and Theodora's panel can be made to answer his. That is why the paired panels work: they are not two moments in one room, they are two statements of equal rank. The real architecture is not missing, it has simply been moved from the picture to the room, and the windows that light the half-dome do the work that a painted building would have done. A viewer standing in the church below is therefore looking at a picture that refuses to be a window and is asking to be read as a presence, and the material is the argument.

questions.explanation: An explanation of this kind has to work in two halves, because the question has two. The first half establishes what the mosaic actually offers the eye: a gold field laid in even courses, no cast shadow, no drawn building, and a real band of windows above the half-dome. From those facts a conclusion can be drawn about the kind of space, because a surface with no cues for distance cannot supply one. The second half then has to say what follows for the subject, and that is where a weak account stops too early. A refusal of depth is not a refusal of meaning. It removes the floor that would make one figure nearer than another, and with the floor gone the size of a figure is free, so an emperor can be made as large as an apse needs. Pair that with the plain fact that the apse stands above an altar, and the apparatus becomes intelligible as a claim about offering rather than about a room. The discipline to hold on to throughout is the separation of what is present from what is inferred: the even gold and the missing shadow are observations, the reading of them is an argument, and a good answer marks which is which rather than blurring the two.
questions.hint: Ask what a surface with no cues for distance can do for a scene that needs to happen somewhere.

questions.topic: Why an illusionistic chapel wall can include a skeleton in a tomb
questions.learningObjective: explain an illusionistic cutaway as a claim about where a viewer stands

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: The method for this question is to take the two structurally different things the picture does in turn, because they pull in opposite directions and the picture is the argument between them. A marginal reminder adds: ask what the hole in the wall is for, and then ask what a body in a coffin at the bottom of it is doing. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: Measured against “explain an illusionistic cutaway as a claim about where a viewer stands / Ask what the hole in the wall is for, and then ask what…”, which answer does the passage sustain?

answer.exemplar: Begin with the fact that a wall is solid, because that is what the painted hole is arguing with. The fresco shows a barrel-vaulted chapel as if the end wall of the church had been cut away: two real piers stand forward, the vault behind them is drawn in correct perspective with its coffers diminishing, and at the back, at the head of the room, is a small painted altar with a standing figure of Christ on the cross, the Virgin on one side and a bearded man on the other. The two donors are painted kneeling outside the painted frame, on the actual wall. So the picture is a join between two kinds of space, a real wall in front and an invented room behind, and the line where they meet is the line the donors occupy. That is where the skill is, and the reason the illusion works. A painted room seen through a painted opening requires the opening to be drawn as a hole and the wall around it to be left solid, and a painter who paints a window where a hole should be gets nothing. The perspective of the vault is not decoration; it is the instrument that measures the distance from the real floor to the painted altar, and it fixes the viewer's place as precisely as a sundial fixes noon. So the first thing the picture does is invite a member of the congregation to stand inside the Trinity, and the kneeling donors show the position that invitation produces. Now the skeleton, which is the part that undoes the invitation. Below the whole illusion, in a painted recess cut into the wall and equal in scale to the real piers, is a human skeleton lying on its back in a sarcophagus with the lid slid off. No attributes, no allegory, no putti: a body, on a slab, in the dark. And it is placed at the bottom, at the level of a real tomb, so it is the most materially convincing thing in the picture. That is the argument. Above, a heaven that opens and lets you in; below, the fate that is the same for everyone, including the two men painted kneeling who are named at the bottom of the wall. Put the two together and the picture is making a claim about time rather than about space, and the means it uses is the collapse of two incompatible scales: the donor is roughly life size and the skeleton is roughly life size, and they are in the same wall. The conclusion is worth stating because it is the kind of thing a cutaway is for. An illusionistic chapel is not a window opened onto a heaven. It is a hole cut through a real wall, and what fills the space behind the hole is a decision about what the viewer believes will be there. Two errors to close. The first is to treat the painted room as a stage set, which misses the point: a stage set is closed and the hole is open, and it is the openness that puts the donor inside. The second is to treat the skeleton as a symbol, as though a skull were a coded message; a skeleton in an open coffin is a statement made with a body, and it needs no translation. The test to apply: ask what the picture would be if the painted piers were removed, and the answer is that it would stop being about this wall and this viewer.

questions.explanation: The method for this question is to take the two structurally different things the picture does in turn, because they pull in opposite directions and the picture is the argument between them. The cutaway is first, and its purpose is to place a viewer. A wall is solid, so a painted room on the face of it can only be looked at. Cut a hole in that wall in paint, and a solid pier stands forward as a real object in front of a receding vault whose coffers diminish in correct perspective, with the actual wall left solid behind the donors. The line where the real wall and the painted room meet is the line the donors kneel on, so the picture joins two kinds of space and puts a member of the congregation inside the second of them. The skeleton is the part that undoes the invitation. A body in an open tomb is the plainest available image of what waits, it is drawn at life size, and it sits at the bottom of the illusion so that the most materially convincing thing in the picture is a corpse. Put the two together and the wall is arguing with itself, and the way it argues is a matter of scale rather than of subject: a donor and a skeleton are the same size and they share a wall. Two errors to close. The cutaway is not a stage set, because a stage set is closed and the hole is open, and the openness is what admits the donor. And the skeleton is not a code to be translated; a body in a coffin is a statement made with a body. The test to apply: ask what the picture would be if the painted piers were removed, and the answer is that it would stop being about this wall and this viewer.

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about what the objects in a domestic annunciation are doing. the question asks two things, and the second is the harder one, so an answer has to tie the ordinary objects to the angel's position and the dropped vessel rather than listing them. A marginal reminder adds: ask whether the angel is arriving or has arrived, and what the untouched state of the room tells you. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: This item turns on “read a group of objects as a statement about a moment / Ask whether the angel is arriving or has arrived, and what the untouched…”. Which of the four options is warranted?

answer.exemplar: The panel shows a workshop room. There is a bench, a table, a fire, a towel on a rod, a candle burnt down, a hanging cloth, a bench, a mouse, and on the sill by the window a small wooden trap with a baited cup and a dead bird beside it; lilies stand in a jug on the table. The angel is coming through an opening in the wall with one knee already across the threshold, and the young woman in the red dress has turned and dropped the jug she was holding. Take the objects first and then the figures, and the design becomes clear. The objects are the reason the panel can be about a moment rather than about a place. Most of them are ordinary, and their ordinariness is load-bearing: a domestic interior is a room where somebody is at work, and the fact that a person is at work in it is what makes the interruption mean something. Two items carry more weight than the rest and they are not the same kind of thing. The lilies are a sign, and a conventional one, and they say who the young woman is without a label. The trap is a different order of object, and it is the most argued-over item on the panel: a small wooden trap with a baited cup and a dead bird, set on a windowsill, has been read as a figure for entrapment and for the danger that waits. Whatever a reader makes of it, the point stands that the painter put a trap in a room where nothing is being trapped, and the placement is doing the work. Now the figures, and here the panel is precise. The angel is not arriving. A knee is through the opening, a wing is inside, and the woman's hand has opened and the jug has gone down and a stream of water is on the floor. So the message has already landed, and the room is caught in the instant after, which is why the towel is still on its rod and the candle has burned low and the work is interrupted rather than finished. That is the formal mechanism that makes the objects legible: they are the residue of a habit that has just been broken. Two errors to close. The objects are not inventory, because a trap on a sill beside a dead bird is a sign and not a possession. And the amount of domestic detail does not make the room the subject, because the subject is what interrupted it, and the panel is about an arrival in a household that was in the middle of a morning.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a Song handscroll is not the painting its attribution names
questions.learningObjective: separate a claim about a design from a claim about a surviving object

stimulus.body: A short reference note on why a song handscroll is not the painting its attribution… is set for a close-reading task. It states: The reasoning here is about the relationship between two kinds of claim, and the method to state is the separation itself. A marginal reminder adds: ask what each piece of evidence is a report about, and how a copy differs from a forgery. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: A reviewer is weighing competing claims about why a song handscroll is not the painting its attribution names, among them "Ask what each piece of evidence is a report about, and…". Based only on the excerpt above, which answer is the one the evidence warrants?

answer.exemplar: Begin by separating the two claims that a name on a scroll usually fuses. The attribution is a claim about a design: it identifies the composition this sheet follows, and it carries with it a history of collecting, mounting and inscription that explains why the sheet is valued. The dating is a claim about an object: the silk has a range, the pigments have ranges, the technique has a range, and a signature by the painter would narrow all of them, and there is none here. Those two claims are compatible once you notice what a copy is. A handscroll that transmits a composition attributed to a fourth-century painter, made seven or eight centuries later by an anonymous workshop, is doing exactly what such workshops did for centuries: preserving a design that the attributed painter could no longer be shown to have executed, and preserving it in a form that readers wanted. So the scroll is not a damaged original and not a forgery. A forgery is a deception, a work made to be taken for something it is not, and nothing here is trying to be that. The strong formulation to reject is that a painting cannot be younger than the artist it is attributed to. That is true of a panel and false of a copy, and the whole distinction is what the case turns on. What the scroll does establish is substantial. It establishes a design in circulation, in a particular state of completeness, with a particular set of episodes, and it establishes that the design was still being copied and collected in the twelfth or thirteenth century, which is itself historical evidence about the prestige of the attribution. It also establishes what the composition is: a narrative handscroll in which a poem is illustrated as a sequence across a continuous landscape, with slender controlled outlines and comparatively light colour washes. The distinction to state at the end is the general one. A name on a label is a report about a history of belief; a support and a pigment analysis is a report about a thing. Ask of each which of the two it is, and the confusion disappears. Where they agree, you have a secure object and a secure design. Where they differ, as here, you have a copy, and the copy is the more interesting evidence, because it dates the design's survival rather than its making.

questions.explanation: The reasoning here is about the relationship between two kinds of claim, and the method to state is the separation itself. A name carried by a scroll is a report about a history of belief: it summarises what collectors, mounting inscriptions and later catalogues concluded, and it identifies a design. A date argued from silk, pigment and technique is a report about a thing in hand. An answer that does not separate them will be pushed into the absurdity that a painting is younger than the artist it names, and the way out is the category of the copy, which makes the separation visible: the scroll transmits a design rather than being an original by the named hand.
questions.hint: Ask what each piece of evidence is a report about, and how a copy differs from a forgery.

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: The area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its height, so the calculation is 68.4 multiplied by 0.5, which is 34.2 square metres. A marginal reminder adds: multiply the two dimensions, then confirm by converting to centimetres and square centimetres. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: The note above supplies the evidence for a judgment about the area of linen in a long embroidered band. One proposed reading is "Multiply the two dimensions, then confirm by converting…". Which of the four options is actually supported by the passage?
questions.explanation: The area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its height, so the calculation is 68.4 multiplied by 0.5, which is 34.2 square metres. The second route gives the same figure independently by scaling both dimensions up by a hundred: 6840 centimetres by 50 centimetres, and 6840 multiplied by 50 is 342,000 square centimetres. A square metre is 10,000 square centimetres, so 342,000 divided by 10,000 is 34.2 square metres, and the two routes agree because the conversion factor cancels against the one it is applied to. A third check is the simplest of all: a height of 0.5 metre is exactly half a metre, so the area is half the length, and half of 68.4 is 34.2. The number matters because of what it implies about the object. Thirty-four square metres of linen is a very large support, and a band of that size cannot be looked at whole by anybody. It has to be read in sections, unrolled a little at a time, which is precisely why the embroidery separates its episodes with written captions: the words are there because the surface is too long for a viewer to hold the sequence in one look. So the arithmetic and the art history are one claim, and a slightly different figure would weaken it: a band of a few metres would not need the apparatus this one has. Note also what the calculation is not. It says nothing about how long the work took, because the rate of stitching is not given, and nothing about how many people worked on it, because the workforce is a separate fact about the commission.
questions.hint: Multiply the two dimensions, then confirm by converting to centimetres and square centimetres.

questions.stem: The controlling cue here is “compute the proportion of two recorded dimensions of a sculpture / Divide the ring's diameter by the total height, multiply by…”. Which option is consistent with it?
questions.explanation: The proportion is the ring's diameter divided by the whole height, multiplied by one hundred, so the calculation is 56.5 divided by 68.3 and then by 100. That quotient is 0.8272327964860908, and one hundred times it is 82.72327964860908, which to one decimal place is 82.7. The same result comes from the reduced form of the fraction: both numbers are given to one decimal place, so multiplying numerator and denominator by ten gives 565 over 683, and 565 divided by 683 is 0.827232796, unchanged, because the scaling cancels. A check by the remaining height does the verification differently again: 68.3 minus 56.5 is 11.8 centimetres, and 11.8 over 68.3 is 0.1727672, whose complement to 1 is 0.8272328, exactly the ratio computed above, so the two parts of the height account for the whole. The figure is worth having because it says something about how the object works. A ring that is 82.7 per cent of the total height is not a background behind the figure; it is a container nearly large enough to hold the whole body, and the figure stands inside it rather than in front of it. That is why the halo is not decoration that could have been made smaller, and why the composition has to be read as a single unit: the ring and the figure are one object, dimensioned together. A proportion near one is the signature of a form in which the enclosure is part of the subject, and this is one of the clearest cases in which two catalogue numbers describe a single idea.
